book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
essays: It’s Only Philosophy but We Like It
The Death of the Woodstock Nation
samples: George A. Reisch's introduction argues that Keith Richards' autobiography Life is more philosophical than Keith's own slogan that rock and roll 'starts from the neck down' allows: its optimistic framing of addiction, arrests, and band feuds displays a distinctive perspective and mental discipline rather than a tale of greed and jealousy. He reads the band's 1990 Prague concert, where Czech fans outlasted Soviet occupation, as evidence that the Stones' music carried a liberating outlook that helped defeat communism or at least outlasted it. The piece sets up the volume's premise that a band proud of its anti-intellectual image nonetheless repays philosophical reading.

Reisch continues the introduction by portraying Keith's devotion to music as a quasi-mystical, life-sustaining focus: his descriptions of guitars weaving with Ronnie Wood's read like a mystic struggling for words, and he would keep playing even without sex, cigarettes, or drink. The section argues the Stones' fifty-year endurance turned them from a youth band into an institution, a rock to lean on, noting that 'Lady Jane' had already punked the older generation and Henry VIII's wives long before the Sex Pistols. Their sheer longevity, surviving Brian Jones's death, Altamont, and heroin, is offered as a fact that should make the philosopher in all of us sit up and take notice.

Reisch recalls Jagger's 1969 reply that he was 'financially dissatisfied, sexually satisfied, and philosophically trying' to argue that the search for satisfaction is a life-long quest rather than a hit single, pointing to the politics of 'Street Fighting Man' and 'Sweet Neo Con', the existentialism of 'Paint it, Black', and 'Sympathy for the Devil' as a dead-serious challenge to the Christian metaphysics of evil. He then compares the band's 1990 Prague concert to Socrates condemned to death for teaching unpopular ideas: the Stones and their fans, like Socrates, outlasted the regime that suppressed them. Eduard Freisler's sobbing father, told by no one after that night how to think, supplies the chapter's closing satisfaction at last.

Randall E. Auxier opens his chapter on the Jagger-Richards collaboration by musing that certain pairs seem 'ordained by the gods' to stay entangled for life, calling Mick and Keith 'destiny's children' who grew up a Stone's throw apart in Dartford. He admits he cannot quite believe in destiny yet claims to have seen cosmic entanglement first hand, and he poses the counterfactual of the two boys taking different buses on the day their collaboration began — a world with no Rolling Stones. The section frames the chapter's question of whether their life-long creative entanglement was inevitable or, as he punningly insists, evitable.

Auxier ranks the Glimmer Twins against other songwriting pairs — Lennon-McCartney as a corporation rather than a cooperation, the Gershwins and John-Taupin as split lyricist-composer teams, Page-Plant and Waters-Gilmour as fellow full collaborations — and argues Mick and Keith matter most philosophically because they 'actually always loved each other', like twin sons of different mothers and a bickering married couple. Citing Christopher Andersen's love-triangle story of the Edith Grove flat, he claims the creative process is inseparable from eros in the ancient sense, with jealousy and envy as its close companions. Two huge personalities locked in one room without blowing up the house is what makes their collaboration so philosophically interesting.

Auxier 'picks a fight' with work-centered philosophy of art, arguing there is no single thing that is 'the' work of art because artworks are living processes tied to their origins, creators, and shifting contexts. 'Street Fighting Man' meant one thing in 1968 and another now, Keith's X-Pensive Winos performances made 'Gimme Shelter' something it previously was not, and Aretha rather than Carole King completed 'A Natural Woman'. He opposes philosophers who study artworks-as-things to those, like himself, who study the creative process, contending that some people — Mick and Keith — can achieve genius only together.

book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
samples: Vannatta's introduction frames the volume with a traffic-intersection metaphor: Klosterman's campaign against the phrase 'guilty pleasure' questions whether the one-way roads of high and low culture are real at all, and the contributors deliberately violate the traffic rules (Kierkegaard meets KISS, Baudrillard meets Britney Spears). It reads Klosterman's line that 'nothing is ever in and of itself' through Kant's noumena-phenomena distinction: like Kant's knowing subject, we never reach the in-itself but only perspectives refracted through rock bands, sports teams, and TV. The introduction presents the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City (identity effaced to imitate an equally constructed identity) and the rock-death road trip of Killing Yourself to Live as Klosterman's way of recovering authenticity, arguing that living with the possibility of one's own death is more authentic than fleeing it.

Auxier argues that Klosterman's signature lists always carry an 'immanent order' of value, illustrated by the twenty-two teenagers' simultaneous classroom thoughts in Downtown Owl and his own contested ranking of the five greatest rock bands. He reads the seventeen-page sober conversation between Julia and Vance, printed with 'what she meant' and 'what he meant' under each remark, through Kant's extensive versus intensive magnitudes: the spoken words are an extensive whole, but the multiple unshared perspectives form an intensive whole no list can exhaust, which is why philosophers crave the 'tug of necessity' that intensive relations never deliver. Plato's Leontius, who rubbernecked at corpses despite his disgust, explains both Klosterman's TMI confessions in Killing Yourself to Live and the 'recoil of the shit-canon' by which we learn to order our desires, while Julia's carbon-monoxide death in the blizzard shows the world converting intensive possibilities into extensive necessity.

Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.

Reisch rebuts Klosterman's Esquire claim that culture, unlike people and movements, can never be wrong because no larger framework stands outside it: he argues something can also go wrong relative to its own internal values, betraying itself as a self-sabotaging painter does. His exhibit is Phil Collins's 'In the Air Tonight', scored by a jokey 'popular music vapidity index' that divides emotional drama by lyrical substance, on which Springsteen's 'Born in the U.S.A.' rates near a healthy 1 while Collins's operatic anguish over a contentless 'it' divides by zero and becomes infinitely vapid. Since the song is beloved cultural wallpaper, its awfulness shows that culture as a whole can betray itself and its members, which is why serious fans feel genuinely let down by hit movies and best-seller lists.

Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.

Vannatta starts from Klosterman's confession that his first dates run on three and a half dates' worth of contrived material, and asks how self-knowledge is possible at all if, as Errol Morris tells Klosterman, we have no privileged access to our own minds. After a tour through Descartes's cogito, Kant's unity of apperception, Freud's unconscious, and Foucault's discourse-constructed subject, the chapter argues with Foucault's Ramist logic of similarity that Klosterman's thought really works by resemblance, mapping his exes onto members of KISS and hearing a dead friend in every Replacements song. Heidegger supplies the resolution: thrown into the crowd's world, we recover ourselves only through its inauthentic pop culture, and Klosterman's 'living is dying, little by little' and obsessive rock-death writing enact being-toward-death as the condition of authenticity.

book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
samples: The editors introduce the volume by reading Gaiman's fiction as travel literature: heroes like Richard Mayhew in Neverwhere, Coraline, and Shadow in American Gods are forced or seduced into enchanted worlds that press against the mundane, and must map and decode those worlds to survive, transforming themselves in the process. They contrast tourists, who stay detached behind camera and guidebook, with travelers, who engage and are changed, and argue that reading Gaiman philosophically turns readers into travelers. They close with Gaiman's Newbery speech about stories as 'good lies that say true things' that leave readers changed forever.

Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.

Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.

Ray Bossert reads American Gods as an allegory of American philosophy: like Gaiman's gods, American philosophers labor invisibly in the background while European publics canonize their thinkers, and Shadow's prison exchanges show the point, since Loki must beg him to read Herodotus ('It's cool') while Johnnie Larch's 'don't piss off people who work in airports' beats Shadow's abstract generalization in usefulness. Following Hickman's Deweyan instrumentalism, he argues the gods are survival tools humans craft from need and discard when obsolete, so Czernobog's hammer gives way to Media's television, Wednesday treats even his own son as an instrument, and the buffalo man's 'believe everything' is advice about keeping one's tools of survival working. The chapter ends on liberty: Shadow refuses to be a god because 'we don't need anyone to believe in us,' and in the Egyptian death trial he claims the most American reward, the freedom to choose his own afterlife.

Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.

T. Bradley Richards takes The Sandman's Dreamworld seriously as a hypothesis: could our nightly dreams be travels to a mind-independent place like Morpheus's realm? Starting from Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Descartes's dream argument, he uses Berkeley's God-sustained idealism as a model for how Morpheus's mind could uphold the Dreamworld's order, and a thought experiment about glitchy dream-travel defuses Descartes's appeal to the discontinuity of dreams. Against the objection that dreams are blatantly contradictory ('it was Dave, but it also wasn't Dave'), he deploys Russell's theory of descriptions against Meinongian subsistence, Chalmers-style conceivability-implies-possibility reasoning from philosophical zombies, and Graham Priest's dialetheism, concluding that dreams could be experiences of an objective world, with waking and dreaming on a par.

book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
samples: The editors' introduction frames Breaking Bad as a recession-era morality play whose overqualified, marginalized Walter White is heir to Macbeth, Faust, and Milton's Lucifer - a fallen anti-hero whose doom we foresee yet whose success we root for. It argues Walt's appeal lies in rebellion against a system that cheated him out of his just reward, while he convinces himself that family, not ego, drives him. The piece surveys the volume's guiding questions: Walt's real motives, his troubled relation to science, the ethics of drugs, existentialism and redemption, Gus Fring as a study in evil, and the show's male-female relationships.

Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.

Sets Walt's 'There's nothing but chemistry here' materialism - the missing 0.111958 percent of the human body that Gretchen calls the soul - against Augustine's Confessions, arguing both men want redemption without giving up their sins: 'give me chastity, but not yet.' It maps Augustine's problem of evil (evil as corruption of the will toward self-destruction) onto Walt's pros-and-cons list over killing Krazy-8 and his 'no-rough-stuff-type deal' fantasy after Tuco. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle then turns chemistry's laws into tendencies, opening room for free choice inside a materialist world - so Walt's remission in 'Over' saves the body, while only changed choices, which he keeps deferring, could save the man.

A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.

Argues Heisenberg is not an alter ego but Walt finally escaping the Prufrock-like bad faith of his pre-cancer life: the pork-pie-hat persona acknowledges the absurd, owns his freedom and responsibility, and so achieves the authenticity Camus and Sartre demand. Walt becomes Camus's Sisyphus - rebelling against death, social norms, and Skyler, owning his rock with silent joy - citing the fulminated-mercury showdown with Tuco in 'Crazy Handful of Nothin'', running down Gus's dealers in 'Half Measures', and confessing to Skyler in 'No Mas'. The chapter closes that, like Sisyphus, we must imagine Walt happy.

Uses Heidegger to read the show's very structure: the pilot's in-medias-res Winnebago crash throws us into Walt's timeline the way Dasein is thrown into time, and the flashbacks to Sandia Labs and 'nowhere to go but up' show his has-been shaping his futurity. Walt's diagnosis makes being-toward-death an overwhelming presence and exposes the failure of his calculative, goal-setting thinking, with the 'Fly' monologue about the perfect moment to die as his turn toward Heidegger's meditative thinking. By dwelling on his own death, the chapter argues, Walt inches toward an authentic being-toward-death - living each moment as if it were his last.

book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
samples: Editor Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that zombies are worth doing philosophy over: an apocalyptic world without government, law enforcement, or private property raises live questions about how survivors should treat one another, whether life becomes 'nasty, brutish, and short', and whether it is wrong to kill a walker. He frames walkers philosophically through Descartes's mindless human-looking automatons and David Chalmers's P-zombies, creatures functionally like us with no inner life. Morgan keeping photo albums instead of supplies in 'Days Gone Bye' shows that what we leave behind after the apocalypse is how we lived - our philosophy.

Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.

Greg Littmann asks whether 'you' survive a walker bite, testing bodily identity, behaviorism, and functionalism as theories of personal survival against Jenner's verdict that after death 'everything you ever were... gone'. His centerpiece adapts Daniel Dennett: survivors yoke walkers to plows and tanks, dangle meat to move them between positions labeled 1 and 0, and gradually build a rope-and-corpse computer functionally identical to a human brain - which behaviorism and functionalism must call conscious, yet which we can conceive as utterly dark inside. The lesson is that we cannot know whether any system, walker, animal, or AI, is conscious, so treatment of non-human systems may need to err on the side of caution.

Richard Greene asks what, if anything, walkers know. Rick's optimistic feeling that Lori and Carl survived turns out true, yet is not knowledge - true belief is necessary but insufficient, the gap Gettier cases exploit - and since walkers can never weigh evidence or think about their thoughts, only externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge can count them as knowers. Walker behavior defeats Jenner's 'mindless instinct' line: Jenny turning the handle of her old house, the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, a walker smashing the department store window with a rock, and the horde seeing through Rick and Glenn's gut disguise once rain washes the scent away. Zombie knowledge is real but limited to simple things recalled from the person's past, the more complex the task the less likely they know it.

Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife is still a person, which decides whether shooting her is murder. On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.

McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.

book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
samples: The editor's introduction argues that Curb-Larry is 'the Larry in all of us': a socially free figure who says what the rest of us repress, from refusing lunch invitations with 'No, I don't really like you that much' to chewing out sample abusers, so that viewers live vicariously through him. Quoting Larry David and Susie Essman on how playing TV-Larry lets the real Larry be more honest ('there's a lack of artifice about TV-Larry'), it frames the book's puzzle: some people hate Curb-Larry because he refuses to pay his dues under the social rules, while others love him because he exposes how dishonestly and un-free their own lives are. It closes by previewing the volume's chapters on ethics, authenticity, religion, race relations, gifts, and Larry's piercing stare.

Ralkowski tests the three classic theories of humor against Curb: Hobbesian superiority (we laugh down at Larry stealing a 5 wood from a corpse or ruining functions), Freudian relief (the rat-dog stomping as released repressed desire, and Larry's deathbed remarks about mayo in 'The End' as gallows humor), and Kantian incongruity (asking Directory Information for 'Krayzee-Eyez Killa,' the vow renewal about bridge tables). Each theory proves either unnecessary or insufficient, so he argues Curb's real engine is what he calls the 'unknown known': the Heideggerian and Wittgensteinian background practices and Searlean social reality we know without knowing we know, like tiptoeing at night or the 'stop and chat.' Larry's jokes work as Mary Douglas's 'anti-rites,' exposing the sheer arbitrariness of unwritten social rules, so comedy at its best both describes and undermines how we live.

Westfall asks whether the Larry we watch is a character or the man himself, since George Costanza was based on Larry yet Curb-Larry insists 'I'm George' and takes Jason Alexander's roast of George personally in 'The Car Salesman.' Sorting the season-seven 'Seinfeld' reunion into three realities—Real, Curb, and Seinfeld—he shows Jason Alexander playing himself playing George while George says Larry's 'pretty, pretty, pretty good' inside a fiction where Larry David does not exist, leaving Larry 'real in fewer ways' than his castmates. The chapter concludes that we can adore and despise Larry at the same moment only because the show makes us treat a non-existent character as real, capped by Larry's catastrophic attempt to play George himself ('There were two Darrens on Bewitched').

Mussell defends Larry's 'idle ideology' against the work ethic that Cheryl, Jeff, and Richard Lewis enforce when they call his car-selling experiment insane or demand he write 'for your own sanity.' Following Weber's story of the Calvinist calling, Russell's In Praise of Idleness, and Adorno's lament that small talk has been assimilated by the utilitarian order, the chapter argues Larry's active idling—leisurely lunches, poker, golf, refusing the 'stop and chat'—reclaims time and makes genuine Socratic conversation possible. His sidewalk ambling and notebook jottings are cast as Benjamin's flaneur and Aristotle's peripatetic strolling, the creative idleness in which Curb's story ideas are born, and the chapter concludes that life's too short to be wasted waiting in line.

Svolba and Flanders read Curb as an extended investigation of civility—the rules of what people 'just don't do,' from using the doctor's phone to touring Susie's new house to singing 'Happy Birthday' at Ben Stiller's party. Larry plays Socratic gadfly: refusing the tour harms no one and treats no one unfairly, and Susie's only justification ('it's just not done') is circular, so his incivility can seem admirable, even like minor civil disobedience. Against this, the chapter argues (crediting Cheshire Calhoun) that rules of civility are conventional vehicles for communicating respect for others' feelings and interests—what matters to Susie ought to matter to Larry—and, more consequentially, that a social world full of Larry Davids would be unbearable. Larry's own Golden-Rule litmus test, by which he never talks in movie theaters because he would hate it himself, misses this point, since civility is precisely about what others happen to want and like.

Mudde and Piercey argue Curb depicts Nietzschean nihilism made humdrum: in Larry's world 'the highest values devalue themselves,' so Ted Danson's 'anonymous' donation is leaked for glory, a terrorist warning becomes leverage in a tiff with Mindy Reiser, and strangers judge everyone constantly because no one is a moral authority. The Platonic and Aristotelian answers to what 'the good' is have no purchase here; moral language survives only as a hollow shell, which is MacIntyre's 'simulacra of morality,' and his own remedy—rebuilding communities that give moral rules a point—fails because on Curb community is hell ('I'd rather have the thieves than the neighbors'). Since ought no longer implies can, the show is tragic, though the Tourettic chef's opening night in 'The Grand Opening,' where Larry leads a communal torrent of obscenities in solidarity, offers a fragile glimpse of doing a little good.

book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
samples: The editors' introduction retells two origin stories of D&D: Gygax and Arneson extending Tolkien fandom and 1970s tabletop wargames, and Gygax's childhood friend Jim Rausch staging live make-believe spy games. It asks whether D&D is a wargame, an art form, or something that resists definition, invoking Wittgenstein's claim that 'game' covers too diverse a range of activities to be defined and Huizinga's Homo Ludens on play standing outside truth and falsity, good and evil. It then frames the volume's guiding questions: whether basement role-playing is mere escapism or a proving ground for ideas, whether players invent new moralities for strange worlds, and what standard of value 'good game' invokes.

Littmann answers the charge that D&D is a waste of time with Aristotle: pleasure is good as an end in itself, humanity's function is thinking, so even munchkin power-gaming and 4E combat roles are worthwhile intellectual activity under the function argument. He then treats D&D as participatory art—improvisational storytelling offering catharsis (smacking goblins to purge aggression) and the Poetics' license to explore what could be, like the dwarf chieftain grieving a disintegrated son or deciding what a friend owes the thief in the scorpion nest. A good DM, on this Aristotelian view, makes plots unfold with internal probability and characters act from consistent personality, yet 'just playing my character' never excuses ruining another player's fun, since artistic value never suspends the virtues governing how we treat people.

Merli argues that good role-playing refutes Aristotelian virtue ethics: decent players convincingly play genuinely evil thieves and morally mediocre players play truly virtuous paladins, so the skill of judging what the virtuous agent would do cannot require being virtuous or having the habituated emotions McDowell, Hursthouse, and Jacobson say are necessary to 'see what to do'. Using a dice-guessing versus unverifiable aura-reading analogy, he shows that the virtue ethicist's escape—denying non-virtuous players can get it right—makes virtuous judgment look fraudulent and untestable. Because role-playing demands active first-person deliberation rather than the passive reception of literary fiction, it exposes that judging rightly and being virtuous are distinct skills, with implications for how habituation and moral education work.

Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.

Bateman replies to Cogburn that Law and Chaos descend not from Kant but from Michael Moorcock's Eternal Champion stories, where they are liberal and conservative political tendencies held in check by the Cosmic Balance, which restores Chaotic Good, Lawful Evil, and the Druid's true Neutral as viable positions. He rejects the 'sausage machine' universalization of maxims for Kant's humanity formula and Realm of Ends, and argues act utilitarianism makes a poor model of Good: an overpopulation scenario could mandate genocide, and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure the good. Alain Badiou's ethic of truths supplies the positive case for Chaotic Good—pursuing what you take to be good without submitting to a single moral law—while Buddhist and Jain renunciation dignifies Lawful Neutral.

Silcox recalls his middle-school Paladin dying to eighty-three orcs while his friends held a memorial service, and asks whether grief for a player character is irrational. He tests Charles Taylor's narrative ethics—the thesis that we grasp our lives as unfolding stories—finding it challenged by Beckett's Godot, the novel-within-a-novel of Atonement, and Samantha Vice's warnings about story-shaped lives, and he notes leveling up and 4E's heroic PCs make characters story-like in ways ordinary lives are not. Ultimately PC death differs from real death because the campaign's story continues without the character, whereas death, as Nagel argues, cuts off our open-ended future; Silcox ends by recasting the self as a 'back-story' or metanarrative that enables storytelling, rejecting Descartes' claim that the power of imagination is inessential to our essence.

book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
samples: Jeopardy! champion Ken Jennings argues that the silly answer-in-the-form-of-a-question conceit is the engine of the show's appeal, because it turns every topic, even Belgium, into a fractal of surprising factual connections rather than a dull definition. He defends the old-school internalization of facts in a Google age - champions are congenitally curious 'sponges' whose stored knowledge makes them better citizens and thinkers - and speculates that what we call the Self is largely the accumulation of facts in one's head. His philosophy of the show in a nutshell: do not just answer in the form of a question, live your life in the form of a question.

Editor Shaun P. Young introduces the volume with a brief history of Jeopardy!, from Merv Griffin's 1964 answer-and-question gimmick (his wife Julann's '5,280 feet') through its record longevity, Emmy wins, pop-culture parodies, and IBM's Watson turning the show into a human-versus-machine spectacle. He frames the book's guiding questions: is Jeopardy! a good game, does it educate or merely entertain, what values does it celebrate, and what can it teach about artificial intelligence and liberal education.

Classicist and Jeopardy! champion Daniel Melia reads the show as a mirror of American exceptionalism, contrasting it with European hits like Big Brother: Jeopardy! is pure individual contest rewarding a faith in classless meritocracy, its Daily Doubles and come-from-behind Final Jeopardy! wagers enact the American belief in redemption and self-reinvention, and its buzzer timing and Before-and-After clues test frontier virtues of physical reflex and improvisation. He argues that its middlebrow categories (Magritte, Sibelius, Paul Revere) preserve shared American cultural capital, and that the show's free-flowing, low-context, information-sharing format answers the question 'What does it mean to be an American, Alex?' and indexes what Americans count as living the good life.

Shaun Young tests Jeopardy! against equality as an 'essentially contested concept': Aristotle's proportional equality (treat like cases as like) seems to justify the winner-take-all payout as deserved, Locke's reward for the industrious explains why equal outcomes would kill incentive, and Rawls's two principles - fair equality of opportunity plus the difference principle - capture the show's identical rules and level playing field. He then raises harder challenges: Dworkin's equality of resources, Kymlicka's charge that the Americo-centric clue bank shortchanges minority cultures (with Quebec's Bill 101 as legitimate differentiated rights), and the capabilities approach of Sen and Nussbaum applied to would-be contestants who cannot operate the signaling device. Citing Isaiah Berlin's pluralism, he concludes that no final verdict on Jeopardy!'s equality is possible - and that spectators would not want one, since Jennings's seventy-four-game streak thrills precisely because of inequality between players.

Brendan Shea argues Jeopardy! is a genuinely good game, building the case on Bernard Suits's The Grasshopper: players pursue a prelusory goal (ending with the most money) through constitutive rules - answering in the form of a question, no buzzing before Trebek finishes, wagers fixed before the clue - obeyed out of a lusory attitude because participants want to play. Good games strike a balance between too easy and impossibly hard so that winning reflects skill rather than luck, which is why the original buzz-anytime rule was revised and why Watson's win impressed where a Wheel of Fortune triumph would not. Playing a good game well matters because it demands and builds real-life skills and, following Hurka and Tasioulas, constitutes an objectively valuable accomplishment animated by a good-making lusory attitude.

Franklin Allaire uses Cliff Clavin's defiant 'Who are three people who've never been in my kitchen?' on Cheers to stage the fight between modern and postmodern theories of knowledge. He rehearses Plato's Theaetetus account of knowledge as justified true belief, Descartes's cogito, and Kant's thing-in-itself as modernity's quest for objective truth via universal intersubjective agreement, then argues through Foucault and Deleuze that Trebek and the judges are gatekeepers whose power controls the narrative - his Civil War renaming example ('What is the War of Northern Aggression?') shows many knowledges competing for one answer. On this view, Cliff's insistence that different questions can fit the same answer exposes the non-objectivity of Jeopardy!'s 'objective' knowledge, making the barfly a postmodern champion.

book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
samples: Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?

Crosby takes Bunk's 'misdemeanor homicide' exchange about Marlo as the show's thesis that post-industrial capitalism makes human lives worth less, season by season devaluing beat cops, longshoremen, would-be reformers, the schoolkids of Season Four, and finally the journalists meant to sound the alarm. She deploys Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how institutions train docile participants and then require their regular sacrifice to keep operating, so that Simon's 'indifferent gods' of Greek tragedy are now postmodern institutions whose lightning bolts hit everyone in the 'hood. She ends with Camus's Sisyphus: Simon's call to commit to a righteous cause you probably will not win is the only response that offers human dignity, because 'this ain't Aruba... this America, man.'

Fagan traces the show's ubiquitous 'Game' to Heraclitus's fragment of Aion as a child moving game-pieces: the drug trade, police, docks, schools, and newsroom all have rules, fixed roles (D'Angelo's chess lecture where pawns get capped quick), winning reduced to stats, strife as justice, and cyclical recurrence with 'new dancers, new faces around the throne.' Bodie's dying rant that the game is rigged, the failed escapes of Wallace, D'Angelo, and Stringer's 'games beyond the game,' and even Omar's fatal loyalty to Butchie show that neither rule-following nor Omar-style code-breaking gets a piece off the board. Against critics who call the show nihilistic, he argues it rejects the Heraclitean picture through Camus's rebellion: Colvin, Bubbles, and Cutty fashion dignity by resisting the Game even though rebellion almost certainly fails.

Allen asks how a virtual war zone can exist inside the United States, starting from Hobbes: Marlo's cool killing of the security guard who just wants to be recognized as a man looks like the rights-free state of nature where 'nothing can be unjust.' But he argues Locke's sharper distinction fits better - the underclass are nominal citizens whose rights to life, policing, and education exist on paper while their substance is denied, which for Locke places an oppressed minority in a state of war within a state, and makes the drug game a rational choice for Michael, Dukie, and Randy. Marlo's 'you want it to be one way, but it's the other way' names that collapsed protection, and the chapter ends with Locke's warning that majority apathy lets oppression persist, reading The Wire as protest art meant to move viewers to political action.

Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.

McAleer ranks three Season-long deceptions - Sobotka's smuggling least wrong, McNulty's fake serial killer worse, Templeton's fabricated Sun stories worst - and argues that only the agents' motives and character explain the degrees of wrongness, against Mill's claim that motive has nothing to do with an action's morality and Kant's distinction between acting in accordance with and from duty. Aristotle's virtue ethics and his difference between practical wisdom and mere cleverness vindicate these verdicts: Sobotka lies to save a dying union, McNulty's cleverness is corrupted by his need to be the smartest boy in the room while Lester's additions lack all wisdom, and Templeton lies from naked careerism with no redemption arc. The chapter closes with the 'Haynes Principle' - 'you need a lot of context to seriously examine anything' - as the case for a messier, character-based moral philosophy.

samples: John Huss's introduction frames the franchise as mirroring successive revolutions: Taylor before the ape tribunal recalls Galileo's heresy trial, the Darwinian revolution that toppled humans from evolution's pinnacle is taken to its logical extreme from Boulle's 1963 novel on, and Rise of the Planet of the Apes stages a 'Molecular Revolution' whose wake-up call is addressed to 'human chauvinists' who forget we share the planet with other species. He reads the cover's interspecies erotica through the Sexual Revolution, quoting Elizabeth Anscombe on contraceptive intercourse and asking whether her argument can get us over the species line, and closes with President Morsi's Tahrir Square allegory of the films: 'We are human, we did do this to ourselves.'

Kristin Andrews uses Taylor's silent attempts to show Zira he has a mind - mouthing answers, wiggling his fingers when she mentions the Hopkins Manual Dexterity Test - to stage the problem of other minds, pushing against Descartes's claim that language is required for thought and Mill's argument from analogy, while Dr. Zaius can always redescribe it all as 'a definite gift for mimicry.' Drawing on her fieldwork with the orangutan Cecep (the leaf-wiping pantomime, guiding the frightened Aldrin home from the turtle scare), she argues against reducing mindreading to false-belief tasks and for knowing minds through shared interaction, inductive overhypotheses, and natural context. She ends with an extended-mind point - 'when you're in a cage, you act caged,' and we offload thinking onto our homes and tools - so lab studies can show what apes can do but never what they can't.

Sara Waller argues the films show language operating as a tyranny that measures minds and withholds moral standing: Dodge mocking signing Caesar as a 'stupid monkey,' Zaius dismissing Taylor's speech as mimicry, 1894 literacy tests used to disenfranchise Black voters, and IQ tests whose vocabulary sections double-count language skill. She surveys the non-linguistic tests the apes face - the Hopkins dexterity test, the Wisconsin Multiphasic, Kohler's banana-and-boxes task ('Because I loathe bananas'), the Lucas Tower, Caesar's cookie-jar deception - and then deploys Quine's 'gavagai' inscrutability of reference to argue that speech cannot be the ultimate measure of intelligence or moral worth. Nova's hand over Taylor's mouth and Zira and Cornelius's 'be clever... be quiet' suggest that under oppression, silence is the smart play.

Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'

Bernard Rollin reads Dr. Zaius's tribunal as 'scientific ideology' in action - 'human see, human do' refuses to believe its own eyes, just as bishops refused to look through Galileo's telescope. He traces the ideology from Newton's 'hypotheses non fingo' through logical positivism's verifiability criterion (which validates the Hasslein Curve prediction while rendering 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven' meaningless) and Wittgenstein's point that 'killing is wrong' is not a fact of the universe, to the 'science is value-free' dogma that left animal pain untested and untreated - as he documents from his own campaign: the empty analgesic literature search, the 1985 federal legislation, and the pain physiologist whose dog research refutes his own denial. Zira's neurosurgery on mute humans repeats what Descartes's beast-machine doctrine licensed, and IASP's language requirement for pain collapses into a Cratylus-grade confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions ('You can't step into the same river once').

Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
